### Q1 — प्रति न्यूक्लिऑन बंधन ऊर्जा वक्र

```
  BE/A
  (MeV)
    9 │                ●  Fe-56  (~8.8 MeV — अधिकतम)
      │            ╱‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾╲____
    8 │        ╱                      ‾‾‾‾‾‾‾‾───────╲ U-238 (~7.6)
      │      ╱  ● O-16
    7 │     ╱
      │    ╱
    6 │   ╱
      │  │ ● He-4 (7.07)
    5 │  │
      │  │
    2 │  ● H-2 (1.1)
      │
    0 └──┴─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┴─────┴────→ A
       0   20    56    100   150   200   238
```

*(दोनों अक्षों पर नाम लिखिए — "प्रति न्यूक्लिऑन बंधन ऊर्जा (MeV)" तथा "द्रव्यमान संख्या A" — और
A ≈ 56 पर शिखर को ≈ 8.8 MeV मान के साथ अंकित कीजिए।)*

**विशेषताएँ:** BE/A हलके नाभिकों के लिए तेज़ी से चढ़ता है, 30 < A < 170 के विस्तृत परिसर में लगभग
**8 MeV पर स्थिर** रहता है, **A ≈ 56 (लोहा) पर लगभग 8.8 MeV का अधिकतम** पाता है, और फिर धीरे-धीरे
गिरकर A = 238 पर लगभग 7.6 MeV हो जाता है।

**दो निष्कर्ष:**

**1. नाभिकीय बल कम परास का है और संतृप्त हो जाता है।** वक्र के अधिकांश भाग में BE/A लगभग स्थिर है,
अर्थात् कुल बंधन ऊर्जा मोटे तौर पर A के समानुपाती है। यदि प्रत्येक न्यूक्लिऑन हर दूसरे को आकर्षित करता,
तो कुल बंधन ऊर्जा A(A − 1)/2 ≈ A² के अनुसार चलती और BE/A, A के साथ रैखिक रूप से बढ़ता। चूँकि ऐसा नहीं
होता, **प्रत्येक न्यूक्लिऑन केवल अपने निकटतम पड़ोसियों से ही क्रिया करता होगा** — नाभिकीय बल कम परास का
है और संतृप्त हो जाता है।

**2. भारी नाभिकों का विखंडन और हलके नाभिकों का संलयन, दोनों ऊर्जा मुक्त करते हैं।** जिन नाभिकों का
**BE/A अधिक है वे अधिक स्थायी हैं**। भारी नाभिक (BE/A ≈ 7.6 MeV) दो मध्यम नाभिकों (BE/A ≈ 8.5 MeV) में
टूटकर वक्र पर **ऊपर** जाता है; दो हलके नाभिकों का संलयन भी बाईं ओर की तीव्र ढलान पर **ऊपर** जाता है।
दोनों स्थितियों में उत्पाद अभिकारकों से अधिक कसकर बद्ध हैं, अतः अतिरिक्त ऊर्जा **मुक्त** होती है।

*(एक तीसरा स्वीकार्य निष्कर्ष: शिखर पर स्थित लोहा-56 सबसे स्थायी नाभिक है — इसीलिए तारों के क्रोड में
नाभिकीय संलयन का अंतिम बिंदु वही है।)*

### Q2 — द्रव्यमान क्षति, बंधन ऊर्जा, और हीलियम का BE/A

**द्रव्यमान क्षति।** नाभिक की **द्रव्यमान क्षति** उसके अवयवी मुक्त न्यूक्लिऑनों के द्रव्यमानों के योग
और नाभिक के वास्तविक द्रव्यमान का अंतर है:

```
      Δm = [ Z m_p + (A − Z) m_n ] − M
```

**बंधन ऊर्जा।** **बंधन ऊर्जा** द्रव्यमान क्षति की ऊर्जा-तुल्य है, BE = Δm c²। यह वह ऊर्जा है जो मुक्त
न्यूक्लिऑनों के जुड़कर नाभिक बनने पर मुक्त होती है, और उतनी ही ऊर्जा नाभिक को पूर्णतः मुक्त
न्यूक्लिऑनों में तोड़ने के लिए देनी पड़ती है।

**⁴₂He के लिए संख्यात्मक** (Z = 2, A = 4, अतः 2 प्रोटॉन और 2 न्यूट्रॉन):

```
      न्यूक्लिऑन द्रव्यमानों का योग = 2 m_p + 2 m_n
                            = 2(1.00728) + 2(1.00867)
                            = 2.01456 + 2.01734
                            = 4.03190 u

      नाभिक का द्रव्यमान       = 4.00151 u
```

**द्रव्यमान क्षति:**

```
      Δm = 4.03190 − 4.00151 = 0.03039 u
```

**बंधन ऊर्जा:**

```
      BE = Δm × 931.5 MeV
         = 0.03039 × 931.5
         = 28.31 MeV
```

**प्रति न्यूक्लिऑन बंधन ऊर्जा:**

```
      BE/A = 28.31/4 = 7.08 MeV
```

**BE/A ≈ 7.08 MeV प्रति न्यूक्लिऑन।**

*(यह लगभग 7.07 MeV के स्वीकृत मान से मेल खाता है, और Q1 के वक्र में आप देख सकते हैं कि ⁴He इतने हलके
नाभिकों की सामान्य प्रवृत्ति से स्पष्ट रूप से ऊपर बैठता है — यह असामान्य रूप से स्थायी नाभिक है।)*

### Q3 — नाभिकीय घनत्व A से स्वतंत्र है

**नाभिक का द्रव्यमान।** द्रव्यमान संख्या A वाले नाभिक में A न्यूक्लिऑन होते हैं, प्रत्येक का द्रव्यमान
लगभग 1 u = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg। अतः

```
      M ≈ A × 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ kg                        अर्थात्  M ∝ A
```

**नाभिक का आयतन।** नाभिक को R = R₀A^(1/3) त्रिज्या का गोला मानने पर:

```
      V = (4/3)π R³ = (4/3)π (R₀ A^(1/3))³ = (4/3)π R₀³ A          अर्थात्  V ∝ A
```

**घनत्व:**

```
      ρ = M/V = ( A × 1.66 × 10⁻²⁷ ) / ( (4/3)π R₀³ A )
```

**अंश और हर के बीच A कट जाता है**:

```
      ρ = (1.66 × 10⁻²⁷) / ( (4/3)π R₀³ )
```

जिसमें **A का कोई उल्लेख ही नहीं** है। अतः नाभिकीय घनत्व **सभी नाभिकों के लिए समान** है। ∎

**इसका मान**, R₀ = 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ m लेकर:

```
      (4/3)π R₀³ = (4/3)(3.1416)(1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵)³
                 = (4.1888)(1.728 × 10⁻⁴⁵)
                 = 7.24 × 10⁻⁴⁵ m³

      ρ = (1.66 × 10⁻²⁷)/(7.24 × 10⁻⁴⁵)
        = 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³
```

**ρ ≈ 2.3 × 10¹⁷ kg m⁻³**, जल के घनत्व का लगभग 10¹⁴ गुना।

**इसका अर्थ:** न्यूक्लिऑन **हर नाभिक में समान रूप से सटकर भरे** हैं, आकार चाहे जो हो — अतः नाभिकीय
पदार्थ वस्तुतः **असंपीड्य** है, और यह स्वयं इसका प्रमाण है कि नाभिकीय बल **संतृप्त** हो जाता है।

### Q4 — नाभिकीय बलों के अभिलक्षण

इनमें से कोई चार:

1. **नाभिकीय परास पर ये ज्ञात सबसे प्रबल बल हैं** — प्रोटॉनों के बीच के स्थिर-वैद्युत प्रतिकर्षण से
   कहीं अधिक प्रबल, इसीलिए बहुत प्रोटॉन वाले नाभिक भी बद्ध रहते हैं।

2. **ये कम परास के हैं।** नाभिकीय बल केवल लगभग **2–3 fm** तक प्रभावी है, और उससे आगे वस्तुतः शून्य।
   (यह स्थिर-वैद्युत और गुरुत्वाकर्षण बलों के तीव्र विपरीत है, जो लंबे परास के हैं।)

3. **ये आवेश-निरपेक्ष हैं।** दो प्रोटॉनों के बीच, दो न्यूट्रॉनों के बीच, और एक प्रोटॉन तथा एक
   न्यूट्रॉन के बीच नाभिकीय बल वस्तुतः **समान** है। अतः यह बल मूलतः विद्युत नहीं है।

4. **ये सामान्य नाभिकीय दूरियों पर आकर्षी हैं पर अत्यंत कम दूरी पर प्रबल प्रतिकर्षी** — लगभग 0.8 fm से
   नीचे बल प्रतिकर्षी हो जाता है, जो नाभिक को ढहने से रोकता है।

5. **ये संतृप्त हो जाते हैं।** कोई न्यूक्लिऑन केवल अपने **निकटतम पड़ोसियों** से क्रिया करता है, नाभिक के
   हर दूसरे न्यूक्लिऑन से नहीं। इसी कारण आवर्त सारणी के अधिकांश भाग में प्रति न्यूक्लिऑन बंधन ऊर्जा
   लगभग स्थिर रहती है।

6. **ये क्रिया करने वाले न्यूक्लिऑनों के चक्रण (spin) पर निर्भर करते हैं**, और **अकेंद्रीय** हैं (वे
   केवल दोनों न्यूक्लिऑनों को जोड़ने वाली रेखा के अनुदिश कार्य नहीं करते)।

### Q5 — विखंडन और संलयन, दोनों ऊर्जा क्यों मुक्त करते हैं

*Q1 के वक्र का संदर्भ दीजिए।*

**नियामक सिद्धांत:** जिस नाभिक की **प्रति न्यूक्लिऑन बंधन ऊर्जा अधिक है वह अधिक कसकर बद्ध और अधिक
स्थायी है**। किसी भी नाभिकीय प्रक्रिया में यदि **उत्पादों का BE/A अभिकारकों से अधिक** है, तो अतिरिक्त
बंधन ऊर्जा अभिक्रिया की ऊर्जा के रूप में **मुक्त** होती है।

**भारी नाभिक का विखंडन।**

यूरेनियम लीजिए, A ≈ 235, BE/A ≈ 7.6 MeV। जब वह A ≈ 120 वाले दो मध्यम-द्रव्यमान खंडों में टूटता है, तो
उन खंडों का BE/A ≈ 8.5 MeV होता है, क्योंकि वे वक्र के समतल मध्य भाग में पड़ते हैं, भारी-नाभिक वाले
सिरे से **ऊपर**।

```
      BE/A में लाभ ≈ 8.5 − 7.6 = 0.9 MeV प्रति न्यूक्लिऑन
      कुल मुक्त ऊर्जा ≈ 0.9 × 235 ≈ 200 MeV
```

अतः खंड जनक नाभिक से अधिक कसकर बद्ध हैं, और प्रति विखंडन लगभग 200 MeV मुक्त होती है।

**दो हलके नाभिकों का संलयन।**

हलके सिरे पर (A < 20) वक्र **बहुत तेज़ी से चढ़ता** है। अतः दो अत्यंत हलके नाभिकों को जोड़ने पर वक्र पर
बहुत **ऊपर** का नाभिक बनता है। उदाहरणार्थ, ड्यूटीरियम का BE/A ≈ 1.1 MeV है जबकि हीलियम-4 का ≈ 7.07 MeV
— लगभग **6 MeV प्रति न्यूक्लिऑन** का लाभ।

अतः उत्पाद अभिकारकों से कहीं अधिक कसकर बद्ध है, और ऊर्जा मुक्त होती है।

**एकीकृत कथन:** दोनों प्रक्रियाओं में उत्पाद अभिकारकों की तुलना में **वक्र के शिखर (A ≈ 56) के अधिक
निकट** पड़ते हैं। विखंडन दाईं ओर से शिखर की ओर A में *नीचे* आता है; संलयन बाईं ओर से शिखर की ओर A में
*ऊपर* जाता है। **ऊर्जा मुक्त करने वाली हर नाभिकीय प्रक्रिया निकाय को A ≈ 56 की ओर ले जाती है।**

*(और प्रति-न्यूक्लिऑन तुलना देखिए: संलयन का ~6 MeV प्रति न्यूक्लिऑन का लाभ विखंडन के ~0.9 MeV से कहीं
अधिक है, इसीलिए प्रति इकाई द्रव्यमान संलयन बहुत समृद्ध ऊर्जा-स्रोत है — भले एक अकेली विखंडन घटना कुल
अधिक ऊर्जा देती है।)*

### Q6 — ऐल्युमिनियम नाभिक की त्रिज्या

```
      A = 27                R₀ = 1.2 fm = 1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵ m
```

```
      R = R₀ A^(1/3)
        = (1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵) × 27^(1/3)
        = (1.2 × 10⁻¹⁵) × 3                    (चूँकि 27^(1/3) = 3)
        = 3.6 × 10⁻¹⁵ m
```

**R = 3.6 × 10⁻¹⁵ m = 3.6 fm**

### Q7 — विखंडन बनाम संलयन

| | **नाभिकीय विखंडन** | **नाभिकीय संलयन** |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **प्रक्रिया** | **भारी** नाभिक तुलनीय द्रव्यमान के दो हलके नाभिकों में **टूटता** है | दो **हलके** नाभिक **जुड़कर** एक भारी नाभिक बनाते हैं |
| **प्रति न्यूक्लिऑन मुक्त ऊर्जा** | लगभग **0.9 MeV** | लगभग **3–7 MeV** — बहुत अधिक |
| **आवश्यक परिस्थितियाँ** | सामान्य ताप पर होता है, मंद न्यूट्रॉन से आरंभ | कूलॉम प्रतिकर्षण पार करने के लिए **अत्यंत उच्च ताप** (~10⁷ K) आवश्यक |
| **नियंत्रणीयता** | **नियंत्रित** किया जा सकता है, जैसे नाभिकीय रिएक्टर में | पृथ्वी पर नियंत्रित करना अत्यंत कठिन |
| **उत्पाद** | रेडियोसक्रिय खंड, जिससे अपशिष्ट-निपटान की समस्या | अधिकतर अरेडियोसक्रिय |

*(कोई तीन पंक्तियाँ 3 अंक का पूरा उत्तर हैं। ध्यान दें कि प्रत्येक पंक्ति दोनों पक्षों में **एक ही**
गुण की तुलना करती है।)*

### Q8 — संलयन को अत्यंत उच्च ताप क्यों चाहिए

दो नाभिकों के संलयित होने के लिए उन्हें एक-दूसरे के लगभग **2 fm** के भीतर आना होगा — आकर्षी
**नाभिकीय बल** का परास।

पर दोनों नाभिक **धनावेशित** हैं, अतः निकट आते समय उन पर प्रबल **स्थिर-वैद्युत प्रतिकर्षण** लगता है जो
1/r² के अनुसार बढ़ता है। यह प्रतिकर्षण कुछ सौ keV कोटि की **कूलॉम विभव रोधिका** बनाता है, जिसे नाभिकों
को अपनी निकट आने की गतिज ऊर्जा से **पार करना** पड़ता है।

बड़ी संख्या में नाभिकों को इतनी गतिज ऊर्जा देने का एकमात्र व्यावहारिक तरीका ताप को अत्यधिक बढ़ाना है,
क्योंकि किसी कण की औसत गतिज ऊर्जा kT की कोटि की होती है। सैकड़ों keV की गतिज ऊर्जा माँगने का अर्थ है
**10⁷ से 10⁹ K** कोटि का ताप।

इसीलिए संलयन को **तापनाभिकीय** अभिक्रिया कहते हैं, और इसीलिए वह प्राकृतिक रूप से केवल **तारों के भीतर**
होता है, जहाँ ऐसे ताप और दाब विद्यमान हैं।

### Q9 — संलयन अभिक्रिया में मुक्त ऊर्जा

```
      ²₁H + ³₁H  →  ⁴₂He + ¹₀n
```

```
      अभिकारकों का द्रव्यमान = 2.014 + 3.016 = 5.030 u
      उत्पादों का द्रव्यमान  = 4.003 + 1.009 = 5.012 u
```

**द्रव्यमान अंतर (द्रव्यमान मात्रकों में Q मान):**

```
      Δm = 5.030 − 5.012 = 0.018 u
```

**मुक्त ऊर्जा:**

```
      Q = Δm × 931.5 MeV
        = 0.018 × 931.5
        = 16.77 MeV
```

**Q ≈ 16.8 MeV**

उत्पादों का द्रव्यमान अभिकारकों से **कम** है, अतः Δm > 0 और ऊर्जा **मुक्त** होती है — अभिक्रिया
ऊष्माक्षेपी है।

### Q10 — सर्वाधिक प्रति न्यूक्लिऑन बंधन ऊर्जा

BE/A वक्र से अधिकतम A ≈ 56 पर है, जो लोहा-56 है (BE/A ≈ 8.8 MeV)।

**उत्तर: (c) ⁵⁶Fe**

*(तुलना के लिए: ⁴He ≈ 7.07 MeV, ²³⁸U ≈ 7.6 MeV, ²H ≈ 1.1 MeV।)*

### Q11 — त्रिज्याओं के अनुपात से द्रव्यमान संख्याओं का अनुपात

```
      R = R₀ A^(1/3)                ⟹      R ∝ A^(1/3)
```

अतः

```
      R₁/R₂ = (A₁/A₂)^(1/3)
⟹     A₁/A₂ = (R₁/R₂)³
```

R₁ : R₂ = 1 : 2 के साथ:

```
      A₁/A₂ = (1/2)³ = 1/8
```

**द्रव्यमान संख्याओं का अनुपात 1 : 8 है।**

### Q12 — प्रकरण अध्ययन: यूरेनियम-235 का विखंडन

```
      ²³⁵₉₂U + ¹₀n  →  ¹⁴¹₅₆Ba + ⁹²₃₆Kr + x ¹₀n + Q
```

**(i) x ज्ञात कीजिए।** **द्रव्यमान संख्या** के संरक्षण का उपयोग कीजिए:

```
      बायाँ पक्ष:  235 + 1 = 236
      दायाँ पक्ष:  141 + 92 + x(1) = 233 + x

      236 = 233 + x
⟹     x = 3
```

**x = 3** — तीन न्यूट्रॉन मुक्त होते हैं।

**(ii) आवेश और द्रव्यमान संख्या के संरक्षण का सत्यापन।**

**आवेश (परमाणु संख्या Z):**

```
      बायाँ पक्ष:  92 + 0 = 92
      दायाँ पक्ष:  56 + 36 + 3(0) = 92          ✓
```

**द्रव्यमान संख्या (A):**

```
      बायाँ पक्ष:  235 + 1 = 236
      दायाँ पक्ष:  141 + 92 + 3(1) = 236        ✓
```

दोनों संरक्षित हैं, जैसा किसी भी नाभिकीय अभिक्रिया में होना ही चाहिए।

**(iii) प्रति न्यूक्लिऑन मुक्त ऊर्जा।**

निहित न्यूक्लिऑनों की कुल संख्या 236 है (²³⁵U और आपाती न्यूट्रॉन मिलाकर):

```
      प्रति न्यूक्लिऑन ऊर्जा = Q/236 = 200/236 = 0.847 MeV
```

**≈ 0.85 MeV प्रति न्यूक्लिऑन**

*(BE/A वक्र के अनुरूप: यूरेनियम लगभग 7.6 MeV पर और खंड लगभग 8.5 MeV पर बैठते हैं, अंतर मोटे तौर पर
0.9 MeV प्रति न्यूक्लिऑन ✓)*

**(iv) शृंखला अभिक्रिया क्यों संभव है।**

अभिक्रिया **एक** न्यूट्रॉन से आरंभ होती है पर **तीन** न्यूट्रॉन मुक्त करती है। उनमें से प्रत्येक
न्यूट्रॉन, यदि उचित रूप से मंदित (moderated) हो जाए और बाहर निकलने या अवशोषित होने के बजाय किसी अन्य
²³⁵U नाभिक से टकराए, तो **आगे एक और विखंडन प्रेरित** कर सकता है, जो बदले में तीन और न्यूट्रॉन मुक्त
करेगा।

अतः विखंडनों की संख्या **एक पीढ़ी से अगली पीढ़ी में गुणित हो सकती है** — एक स्वतःपोषी
**शृंखला अभिक्रिया**। यदि गुणन को ठीक एक विखंडन प्रति विखंडन पर रोक दिया जाए (नियंत्रक छड़ों से अतिरिक्त
न्यूट्रॉन अवशोषित करके), तो अभिक्रिया **नियंत्रित** होती है, जैसे नाभिकीय रिएक्टर में। यदि उसे बढ़ने
दिया जाए, तो मुक्ति विस्फोटक हो जाती है।

### Q13 — नाभिकीय घनत्वों का अनुपात

**नाभिकीय घनत्व द्रव्यमान संख्या से स्वतंत्र है** (जैसा Q3 में दिखाया गया), क्योंकि द्रव्यमान A के
समानुपाती है और आयतन भी A के समानुपाती है, अतः उनका अनुपात एक नियतांक है।

अतः द्रव्यमान संख्याएँ चाहे जो हों,

```
      ρ₁ : ρ₂ = 1 : 1
```

**नाभिकीय घनत्वों का अनुपात 1 : 1 है** — वे बराबर हैं।

*(द्रव्यमान संख्याओं का 8 : 125 अनुपात भटकाने वाला है। वह **त्रिज्याओं** के अनुपात के लिए महत्वपूर्ण
होता, जो (8/125)^(1/3) = 2 : 5 होगा।)*

plan.body:
Two plans. Pick by how much time is left.

- **Plan A — Full session (April → February).** The one to follow if you are starting on time.
- **Plan B — 100 days.** If you are starting in November/December.
- **Plan C — 30 days.** Triage. Read the honesty note before using it.

All plans assume board exams in **late February / March**, with pre-boards in **December/January**.

---

## The two rules that matter more than the plan

**Rule 1 — Learn a chapter, then immediately do its PYQs.** Not "finish the syllabus, then start
PYQs in January". A chapter you learnt in June and first tested in January is a chapter you will
learn twice. Every chapter note in this repo has its PYQ set attached for exactly this reason.

**Rule 2 — Revise on a schedule, not on a feeling.** After finishing a chapter, revisit it at
**day 7** and **day 30** — 20 minutes each time, formula box plus two hard PYQs. Two short revisits
beat one long re-read, by a wide margin. Keep a table:

| Chapter | Learnt | Day-7 revisit | Day-30 revisit | Test score |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| M-05 Continuity & Diff. | 12 Jun | 19 Jun | 12 Jul | 82% |

That table is your actual study plan. Everything below is just the first column.

---

## Plan A — Full session

### Sequencing logic

Maths and Physics are studied **in parallel**, not one then the other, because school teaches them
in parallel and because Physics needs calculus you learn in Maths.

Two ordering choices are deliberate:

- **Maths starts with Matrices/Determinants, not Chapter 1.** Relations & Functions is abstract and
  is a poor confidence-builder in April. Algebra is mechanical, scores fast, and is only 10 marks —
  finish it early and it never worries you again.
- **Physics follows book order (Electrostatics → Semiconductors).** Physics genuinely builds:
  potential needs field, EMI needs magnetism, AC needs EMI. Don't reorder Physics.

### Term 1: April → September (finish 80% of syllabus)

| Weeks | Maths | Physics |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Apr, wk 1–2** | Ch 3 Matrices · Ch 4 Determinants | Ch 1 Electric Charges and Fields |
| **Apr, wk 3–4** | Ch 1 Relations and Functions · Ch 2 Inverse Trig | Ch 2 Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance |
| **May, wk 1–2** | Ch 5 Continuity and Differentiability | Ch 2 (cont.) · Ch 3 Current Electricity |
| **May, wk 3–4** | Ch 5 (cont.) · Ch 6 Application of Derivatives | Ch 3 (cont.) — **Unit I+II done (16 marks)** |
| **Jun, wk 1–2** | Ch 6 (cont.) | Ch 4 Moving Charges and Magnetism |
| **Jun, wk 3–4** | Ch 7 Integrals — start | Ch 4 (cont.) · Ch 5 Magnetism and Matter |
| **Jul, wk 1–2** | Ch 7 Integrals — indefinite, all methods | Ch 6 Electromagnetic Induction |
| **Jul, wk 3–4** | Ch 7 Integrals — definite, properties | Ch 7 Alternating Current |
| **Aug, wk 1–2** | Ch 8 Application of Integrals | Ch 7 (cont.) — **Unit III+IV done (17 marks)** |
| **Aug, wk 3–4** | Ch 9 Differential Equations | Ch 8 EM Waves · Ch 9 Ray Optics — start |
| **Sep, wk 1–2** | Ch 10 Vector Algebra | Ch 9 Ray Optics — lenses, prism |
| **Sep, wk 3–4** | Ch 11 Three Dimensional Geometry | Ch 9 Ray Optics — instruments |

**Milestone, end of September:** Maths Ch 1–11 done (75 of 80 marks covered). Physics Ch 1–9 done
(about 50 of 70 marks). Half-yearly exams fall here — treat them as a real dress rehearsal.

### Term 2: October → December (finish syllabus + first full revision)

| Weeks | Maths | Physics |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Oct, wk 1–2** | Ch 12 Linear Programming · Ch 13 Probability | Ch 10 Wave Optics — **Unit V+VI done (18 marks)** |
| **Oct, wk 3–4** | **Syllabus complete.** Revision round 1: Unit III Calculus | Ch 11 Dual Nature · Ch 12 Atoms |
| **Nov, wk 1–2** | Revision round 1: Algebra, Vectors & 3D | Ch 13 Nuclei · Ch 14 Semiconductor Electronics — **syllabus complete** |
| **Nov, wk 3–4** | Revision round 1: Relations, LP, Probability | Revision round 1: Electrostatics + Current Electricity |
| **Dec, wk 1–2** | Full 80-mark mock #1, self-scored against marking scheme | Revision round 1: Magnetism + EMI + AC |
| **Dec, wk 3–4** | Mock #2 + error log review | Revision round 1: Optics + Modern Physics + Semiconductors, full 70-mark mock #1 |

**Milestone, end of December:** whole syllabus covered once, revised once, two full mocks per subject
written under exam conditions. Pre-boards will now be a formality rather than a shock.

### Term 3: January → February (PYQs and mocks only — no new learning)

| Weeks | Both subjects |
| --- | --- |
| **Jan, wk 1** | Last 5 years' board papers, one per day, timed, alternating subjects |
| **Jan, wk 2** | Years 6–10 of PYQs. Maintain the **error log** (see below) |
| **Jan, wk 3** | CBSE official sample paper + 3 more mocks each. Re-derive the full [derivations list](../physics/derivations-list.md) on blank paper |
| **Jan, wk 4** | Revision round 2, driven *entirely* by the error log — only weak topics |
| **Feb, wk 1–2** | Mocks every alternate day. Formula sheets daily, 20 min each subject |
| **Feb, wk 3** | Formula sheets, marking-scheme language, error log. **Nothing new.** Sleep normally |

### Weekly rhythm inside Plan A

Assume ~3 hours/day on these two subjects (the rest of the day belongs to your other three subjects).

| Day | Maths | Physics |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Mon | 1 h new topic | 1 h new topic + 30 min numericals |
| Tue | 1 h new topic + 30 min PYQs | 1 h new topic |
| Wed | 1 h new topic | 1 h new topic + 30 min derivation practice |
| Thu | 1 h PYQs | 1 h PYQs |
| Fri | 1 h new topic | 1 h new topic |
| Sat | 90 min: chapter test from these notes | 90 min: chapter test from these notes |
| Sun | 60 min: day-7 and day-30 revisits (both subjects). Rest of the day off | — |

Sunday off is part of the plan, not a failure of it.

---

## Plan B — 100 days (starting ~mid-November)

You cannot cover everything at equal depth. Cover everything at *unequal* depth, deliberately.

### Days 1–45: high-weightage core

**Maths (in this order):**
1. Ch 7 Integrals (the single largest source of marks in the paper)
2. Ch 5 Continuity and Differentiability
3. Ch 3 Matrices + Ch 4 Determinants (fast, mechanical, 10 marks)
4. Ch 6 Application of Derivatives
5. Ch 10 Vector Algebra + Ch 11 3D Geometry (14 marks, very formula-driven — high return)
6. Ch 9 Differential Equations
7. Ch 13 Probability + Ch 12 Linear Programming (13 marks, both small)
8. Ch 8 Application of Integrals
9. Ch 1 + Ch 2 (8 marks, mostly MCQ-level after deletions)

**Physics (in this order):**
1. Ch 9 Ray Optics (largest single chapter)
2. Ch 3 Current Electricity
3. Ch 2 Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance
4. Ch 7 Alternating Current + Ch 6 EMI
5. Ch 4 Moving Charges and Magnetism
6. Ch 10 Wave Optics
7. Ch 14 Semiconductor Electronics (7 marks, tiny syllabus — do not skip)
8. Ch 11 Dual Nature + Ch 12 Atoms + Ch 13 Nuclei
9. Ch 1 Electric Charges and Fields
10. Ch 5 Magnetism and Matter + Ch 8 EM Waves (small after deletions, mostly 1–2 markers)

For each chapter: *Brief* → formula box → *PYQs with solutions* → *Test yourself*. Skip nothing
inside a chapter you have decided to do; a half-learnt chapter scores worse than a skipped one
because it eats the same time.

### Days 46–75: PYQs

Last 10 years, chapter-wise first (all Integrals questions together, all Optics questions together —
pattern recognition builds far faster this way), then 6 full papers per subject in chronological order.

### Days 76–100: mocks and the error log

One full paper every alternate day, alternating subjects. Score it yourself, harshly. Every dropped
mark goes in the error log. Final week: error log + formula sheets only.

---

## Plan C — 30 days (triage)

**Be honest about what this is.** In 30 days you are playing for a solid pass and a decent
percentage, not for 95. That is a perfectly reasonable goal, and the way to hit it is ruthless
prioritisation — not trying to do everything badly.

### The 60% rule

Roughly 60% of both papers comes from a minority of the syllabus. Target that, completely.

**Maths — the 30-day list (~55 of 80 marks):**

| Do completely | Marks reachable |
| --- | --- |
| Ch 7 Integrals: standard forms, substitution, by parts, partial fractions, definite-integral properties | ~12 |
| Ch 3 + Ch 4: inverse of 3×3, solving equations by matrix method, adjoint, properties | ~10 |
| Ch 10 + Ch 11: dot/cross product, projection, angle, line equations, shortest distance | ~14 |
| Ch 13 Probability: conditional probability, total probability, Bayes | ~8 |
| Ch 12 Linear Programming: graphical method, corner-point rule | ~5 |
| Ch 5: continuity at a point, differentiability, chain rule, implicit, logarithmic | ~6 |

**Physics — the 30-day list (~45 of 70 marks):**

| Do completely | Marks reachable |
| --- | --- |
| Ch 9 Ray Optics: mirror/lens formula, refraction, prism, TIR, microscope + telescope | ~10 |
| Ch 3 Current Electricity: Ohm's law, drift velocity, resistivity, cells in series/parallel, Kirchhoff, Wheatstone | ~7 |
| Ch 2 Potential & Capacitance: potential due to charge/dipole, equipotentials, capacitance, dielectric, energy | ~6 |
| Ch 7 AC: LCR series, impedance, resonance, power factor, transformer | ~6 |
| Ch 14 Semiconductors: whole chapter | ~7 |
| Ch 10 Wave Optics: YDSE fringe width, single-slit diffraction, polarisation | ~5 |
| Ch 11 Dual Nature: photoelectric effect, Einstein's equation, de Broglie | ~4 |

### 30-day shape

- **Days 1–18:** the lists above, roughly one chapter per 2 days, brief + formulas + PYQs.
- **Days 19–25:** last 5 years' PYQs, chapter-wise, restricted to the topics you studied.
- **Days 26–29:** two full mocks per subject. Attempt *everything*, including topics you skipped —
  MCQs from unstudied chapters are often guessable, and Assertion–Reason often is too.
- **Day 30:** formula sheets. Sleep 8 hours.

### What you are giving up

Relations & Functions proofs, Application of Integrals, Differential Equations beyond the linear
form, Magnetism and Matter, Atoms and Nuclei derivations, EM Waves detail. You will lose marks
there. Attempt their MCQs anyway.

---

## The error log — the highest-return habit in this document

One page per subject, maintained from day one. For every mark you drop in any test:

| Date | Q | Chapter | What went wrong | Category |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 14 Jan | 32 | M-07 Integrals | Forgot to change limits after substitution | **Method** |
| 14 Jan | 28 | P-09 Optics | Sign convention: took u positive | **Concept** |
| 16 Jan | 21 | M-04 Determinants | Arithmetic slip in cofactor | **Careless** |
| 16 Jan | 33 | P-07 AC | Didn't draw the phasor diagram | **Presentation** |

Four categories, and each has a different fix:

- **Concept** — go back to the chapter *Brief*. This is the only category that needs re-learning.
- **Method** — you knew the concept but not the standard procedure. Drill 5 more of the same type.
- **Careless** — arithmetic, transcription, sign slips. Fix by *slowing down the first line* of every
  question, not by working more problems.
- **Presentation** — missing diagram, missing unit, no final statement, unlabelled graph. Free
  marks. Fix by re-reading section 4 of the [blueprint](00-exam-blueprint.md) once a week.

In the last two weeks, count your categories. If most entries are *Careless* or *Presentation*, you
do not need more study — you need slower, more disciplined writing. Most students in February get
this diagnosis exactly backwards and study more when they should be writing more carefully.

---

## Practical / internal assessment — 20 (Maths) + 30 (Physics)

Fifty marks, and they are the easiest fifty in the year. Do not treat them as an afterthought.

- **Physics practical file:** write it up as you go, not the week before. Each experiment needs aim,
  apparatus, theory with formula, diagram, observation table, calculation, result with error, and
  precautions. The diagram and the observation table are where marks are actually lost.
- **Physics viva (5 marks):** the examiner asks about the *theory* of your experiments — least count,
  why zero error matters, the formula's origin. Know the theory of every experiment in your file.
- **Physics investigatory project (3 marks):** choose something you can explain in two minutes.
- **Maths portfolio and activities (10 marks):** neatness and completeness are the whole mark. Hand
  it in on time.
- **Periodic tests (Maths, 10 marks):** these are averaged. A bad September test costs you board
  percentage. Take each one seriously.

answer.body:
The blueprint tells you what the paper looks like. This tells you what to *write*.

Each question type below has a fixed template. Learn the template and you stop making decisions
under time pressure — which is where marks go.

---

## Universal rules

1. **Formula → substitution → answer.** Three lines, every numerical, both subjects. The middle line
   is where the method marks live.
2. **Draw the diagram, always.** Even when unasked. A ray diagram, circuit, phasor diagram,
   feasible region, or shaded-area sketch carries its own ½–1 mark and is awarded independently.
3. **Units in Physics, arrows on vectors in Maths.** Both cost ½ mark each time.
4. **Never leave a question blank.** Write the formula. Write what is given. Partial method marks are
   real, and Assertion–Reason/MCQs have no negative marking.
5. **Underline or box the final answer**, and state it as a sentence when the question asked in words
   ("Hence the focal length is 20 cm").

---

## Section A — MCQs (1 mark)

**Time: 45 seconds each. Hard limit.**

- Do not solve fully if you can eliminate. Check units, signs, limiting cases, and order of magnitude.
- **Physics dimension trick:** if options differ in units or dimensions, dimensional analysis alone
  usually settles it without any physics.
- **Maths:** substitute a convenient value (x = 0, 1, or π/2) into the given and the options.
- Circle the option letter **and** write the option's content. If the letter is ambiguous the
  examiner reads the content.
- Anything taking over 90 seconds: mark it, move on, come back. Never sink 5 minutes into 1 mark.

## Section A — Assertion–Reason (1 mark)

The standard four options:

- (a) Both A and R true, and R **is** the correct explanation of A
- (b) Both A and R true, but R is **not** the correct explanation of A
- (c) A true, R false
- (d) A false, R true

**Method — three separate judgements, in this order.** Do not shortcut it.

1. Is A true, on its own?
2. Is R true, on its own? (R is often a correct textbook statement that is simply irrelevant.)
3. Only if both are true: does R *cause/explain* A?

The trap is almost always at step 3 — two true statements where R explains something else. When both
are true and you are genuinely unsure whether R explains A, **(a) is more often correct than (b)** in
CBSE papers. Use that only as a tiebreak, never as a substitute for step 3.

## Section B — Very Short Answer (2 marks)

**Two marks = two scoring points.** Find them before writing.

- "State X and write its SI unit" → the statement is 1, the unit is 1. Both, explicitly.
- "Define X. Write its dimensional formula." → same structure.
- A 2-mark numerical → formula (1) + substitution and answer with unit (1).
- A 2-mark "why/how" → the reason (1) + the consequence (1).

**Do not over-write.** A 2-mark answer is 2–4 lines. Writing half a page earns nothing extra and
costs you time in Section E. This is the single most common time leak in Physics.

## Section C — Short Answer (3 marks)

**Three marks = three scoring points**, and in Physics one of them is very often the diagram.

Typical splits:
- Physics derivation: diagram (1) + set-up (1) + result (1)
- Physics numerical: formula (1) + substitution (1) + answer with unit (1)
- Maths integral: correct method choice/substitution (1) + integration (1) + simplification and `+C` (1)
- Maths "prove that": start from LHS (1) + key manipulation (1) + reach RHS with a concluding line (1)

Always end a proof with an explicit closing line — "= RHS, hence proved". The examiner looks for it.

## Section D (Physics) / Section E (Maths) — Case-study (4 marks)

- **Read the passage last.** Read the sub-questions first, then mine the passage for exactly the
  numbers you need. Reading the passage first wastes 90 seconds.
- Sub-parts are independent. Getting (i) wrong does not stop you scoring (ii), (iii), (iv) — unless
  you carry a wrong number forward, so recompute rather than reuse when it's cheap.
- The last sub-part usually has an internal choice (OR). Read both, pick fast, **cross out the one
  you abandoned**.
- Answers here are short — one or two lines each. Do not write essays.

## Section E (Physics) / Section D (Maths) — Long Answer (5 marks)

The highest-value questions in the paper, and the most template-driven.

**Physics 5-marker — the fixed order:**
1. **Labelled diagram** (½–1 mark) — ray diagram, circuit, phasor, field lines. First, before any algebra.
2. **State the principle or law** you are using, in words (½ mark).
3. **Set up** the governing equation from that law (1 mark).
4. **Derive** — every algebraic step, no jumps (1½–2 marks).
5. **Box the result**, and state what each symbol means if you introduced new ones (½ mark).
6. **Then** do the numerical or application part, formula → substitution → answer with unit.

If you are stuck on the algebra, write steps 1, 2 and 5 anyway — the diagram, the law, and the known
final result. That is often 2 of 5 marks recovered from a question you could not do.

**Maths 5-marker — the fixed order:**
1. Write what is given, in symbols.
2. Name the method in one line ("Using integration by parts with u = …, dv = …", "By matrix method,
   AX = B so X = A⁻¹B").
3. Full working, one step per line. Never combine two algebraic moves on one line.
4. For area problems: sketch the region and shade it *before* integrating, and write the limits with
   a one-line justification of where they came from (the intersection points).
5. Final answer boxed, with units if the problem had them (cm², cubic units, etc.).

---

## Subject-specific patterns worth memorising

### Physics: the "derive + numerical" hybrid

Most 5-markers are `derivation (3) + numerical using that result (2)`. Students derive well and then
run out of time on the numerical, or skip the derivation to reach the numerical. Do the derivation
properly — it is the bigger half — and give the numerical its three lines.

### Physics: graph questions

Every graph answer needs **both axes labelled with quantity and unit**, the shape correct, and any
intercept/slope/asymptote marked. Common ones: photoelectric (stopping potential vs frequency;
current vs potential for different intensities), V–I for a diode, impedance vs frequency for LCR,
binding energy per nucleon vs mass number, resistivity vs temperature for conductor/semiconductor.
Learn the *intercept meaning* of each — that is what gets asked.

### Physics: "distinguish between" questions

Answer in a **two-column table**, three points minimum, comparing the *same* attribute on each row.
Comparing different attributes on each side scores badly.

### Maths: integration — choose the method in the first 15 seconds

| If the integrand looks like | Try |
| --- | --- |
| f(g(x))·g'(x) | substitution |
| product of unrelated functions | by parts, ILATE order |
| rational, denominator factorises | partial fractions |
| 1/(quadratic) or 1/√(quadratic) | complete the square → standard form |
| involves √(a²−x²), √(a²+x²), √(x²−a²) | trig substitution x = a sinθ, a tanθ, a secθ |
| definite, limits symmetric about 0 | check odd/even property first |
| definite, limits 0 to a | try the f(x) → f(a−x) property |

Spending 15 seconds classifying beats 5 minutes of a wrong method.

### Maths: Bayes' theorem — the fixed layout

Always write it as: define events → write all priors P(Eᵢ) → write all likelihoods P(A|Eᵢ) → write
the formula → substitute. Laid out that way, you cannot mix up numerator and denominator, which is
the standard way this question is lost.

### Maths: Linear Programming — the fixed layout

1. Tabulate constraints and write them as inequalities, including x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0.
2. Draw the graph on **graph paper**, scale stated, lines labelled with their equations.
3. Shade the feasible region and **name every corner point with its coordinates** (solve the
   simultaneous equations to get them — do not read them off the graph).
4. Table of Z at each corner point.
5. State max/min, at which point, and whether the region is bounded. If unbounded, do the extra
   check (test whether the open half-plane Z > max, or Z < min, has any common point with the
   feasible region) — this is the mark most students lose.

---

## The last 10 minutes

Do not start a new question. Instead:

1. Check every numerical has a **unit**.
2. Check every vector answer has an **arrow or î ĵ k̂ form**.
3. Check every graph has **labelled axes**.
4. Check you crossed out abandoned internal-choice attempts.
5. Check question numbers match the paper.
6. Check every `∫` in an indefinite integral ended with **`+ C`**.

That checklist is worth 3–5 marks in a typical paper. It is the cheapest revision you will ever do.

pyqm.body:
Read [`README.md`](README.md) in this folder for how the Freq and Priority bands are defined and what
they are and are not.

Only **current-syllabus** topics appear here. Deleted topics (composite/invertible functions, inverse
trig identities, tangents & normals, area between two curves, planes in 3D, Binomial distribution,
and the rest) are listed in [`../docs/00-exam-blueprint.md`](../docs/00-exam-blueprint.md) §3.

---

## The 60-mark core

If you learn nothing else, learn these fourteen question types. Together they have historically
covered around 60 of 80 marks.

| # | Question type | Chapter | Marks | Freq |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Solve 3 linear equations by matrix method (X = A⁻¹B) | 4 | 5 | Every year |
| 2 | Integration by partial fractions | 7 | 3–5 | Every year |
| 3 | Bayes' theorem word problem | 13 | 4–5 | Every year |
| 4 | Linear differential equation, dy/dx + Py = Q | 9 | 3–5 | Every year |
| 5 | Maxima–minima word problem | 6 | 4–5 | Every year |
| 6 | Shortest distance between two skew lines | 11 | 3–5 | 9/10 |
| 7 | Continuity at a point — find k | 5 | 2–3 | Every year |
| 8 | Definite integral using the f(x) → f(a−x) property | 7 | 3 | 9/10 |
| 9 | Linear programming, graphical, corner-point | 12 | 4–5 | Every year |
| 10 | Area bounded by a line and a circle/parabola | 8 | 5 | 8/10 |
| 11 | Prove a relation is an equivalence relation | 1 | 2–3 | 8/10 |
| 12 | Projection / angle / area using dot and cross product | 10 | 2–3 | Every year |
| 13 | Logarithmic or implicit differentiation | 5 | 3 | Every year |
| 14 | Integration by parts (ILATE) | 7 | 3 | Every year |

---

## Unit I — Relations and Functions (8 marks)

### Ch 1. Relations and Functions

| Topic | Marks | Freq | Priority |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Check reflexive / symmetric / transitive for a given relation | 2–3 | Every year | **P1** |
| Prove a relation is an equivalence relation; find an equivalence class | 3–5 | 8/10 | **P1** |
| Prove a function is one-one and onto (bijective) | 3–5 | 7/10 | **P1** |
| Counting: number of relations / functions / one-one functions on a small set | 1 | 7/10 | P2 |
| Identify from a graph or arrow diagram whether a function is injective/surjective | 1 | 5/10 | P2 |
| Modify domain/codomain to make a function bijective | 1–2 | 4/10 | P3 |

**Pattern note.** After the deletion of composition and invertible functions, this chapter shrank
sharply. What remains is highly stereotyped: a relation defined by "a − b is divisible by n", or
"|a − b| is even", or on a set of triangles/lines, and you must classify it. And a function like
f(x) = (4x+3)/(6x−4) or f(x) = x² on a restricted domain, to be shown bijective.

**The trap.** For *transitive*, students test one example and declare it transitive. Transitivity
must be argued in general — take arbitrary (a,b) and (b,c) in R and show (a,c) ∈ R. For a *counter*
example, one concrete pair is enough and that asymmetry is exactly what CBSE tests.

### Ch 2. Inverse Trigonometric Functions

| Topic | Marks | Freq | Priority |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Principal value of sin⁻¹ / cos⁻¹ / tan⁻¹ of a given number | 1–2 | Every year | **P1** |
| Domain and range (principal value branch) of an inverse trig function | 1 | Every year | **P1** |
| Evaluate a composite like sin(cos⁻¹ x), tan(sin⁻¹ x) | 1–2 | 7/10 | P2 |
| Evaluate sin⁻¹(sin θ) / cos⁻¹(cos θ) where θ is *outside* the principal branch | 1–2 | 8/10 | **P1** |
| Sum/simplify two inverse trig terms | 2 | 4/10 | P3 |

**Pattern note.** Now almost entirely a Section-A chapter. The single most-asked idea is
sin⁻¹(sin θ) for θ outside [−π/2, π/2] — e.g. sin⁻¹(sin(3π/4)) = π/4, not 3π/4. It appears as an
MCQ nearly every year because it separates students who memorised "they cancel" from students who
know the range.

---

## Unit II — Algebra (10 marks)

### Ch 3. Matrices

| Topic | Marks | Freq | Priority |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Find unknowns from a matrix equation (equate corresponding elements) | 1–2 | Every year | **P1** |
| Symmetric / skew-symmetric: identify, or express A as sum of both | 2–3 | 8/10 | **P1** |
| Compute AB, verify (AB)ᵀ = BᵀAᵀ | 2 | 7/10 | P2 |
| Order of a matrix / number of elements / number of possible matrices | 1 | 8/10 | P2 |
| A² = A or A² = I type: find the matrix or a scalar | 2–3 | 6/10 | P2 |
| Diagonal elements of a skew-symmetric matrix are zero (as MCQ/AR) | 1 | 6/10 | P2 |
| Transpose and its properties | 1–2 | 6/10 | P2 |

**Pattern note.** With elementary row operations deleted, matrix inversion moved fully into
Determinants (via adjoint). What is left in Ch 3 is arithmetic and the symmetric/skew-symmetric
structure — quick marks, and often in Section A or B.

### Ch 4. Determinants

| Topic | Marks | Freq | Priority |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Solve a system of 3 equations by matrix method | 5 | Every year | **P1** |
| Find A⁻¹ using adj A for a 3×3 matrix | 3–5 | Every year | **P1** |
| Verify A(adj A) = |A|I | 2–3 | 6/10 | P2 |
| |kA| = kⁿ|A|, |adj A| = |A|ⁿ⁻¹, |A⁻¹| = 1/|A| | 1 | Every year | **P1** |
| Area of a triangle / collinearity of three points by determinant | 1–2 | 7/10 | P2 |
| Value of x from a given determinant equation | 1–2 | 7/10 | P2 |
| Consistency / inconsistency of a system from |A| and (adj A)B | 1–3 | 5/10 | P2 |
| Cofactor / minor of a specific element | 1 | 6/10 | P2 |

**Pattern note.** This is the most reliable 5-mark question in the entire paper. The system-of-three-
equations question has appeared in essentially every session for a decade, sometimes dressed as a
word problem (three people buying three items; award money split three ways). The dressing changes;
the method never does.

**The trap.** Students compute adj A but forget it is the transpose of the cofactor matrix, and skip
the transpose step. Also: the sign pattern `+ − + / − + − / + − +` for cofactors. Both cost the whole
question.

---

## Unit III — Calculus (35 marks) — the half of the paper

### Ch 5. Continuity and Differentiability

| Topic | Marks | Freq | Priority |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Find k / a / b so a piecewise function is continuous at a point | 2–3 | Every year | **P1** |
| Logarithmic differentiation — y = xˣ, xʸ = yˣ, y = (f)^(g) | 3 | Every year | **P1** |
| Implicit differentiation | 2–3 | Every year | **P1** |
| Parametric differentiation (x = f(t), y = g(t)) | 2–3 | 8/10 | **P1** |
| Second-order derivative; prove a relation like (1−x²)y″ − xy′ − a²y = 0 | 3–5 | 8/10 | **P1** |
| Differentiability at a point / continuity ⇏ differentiability | 1–2 | 7/10 | P2 |
| Chain rule on a composite of 3 functions | 2 | Every year | **P1** |
| Continuity of |x|, [x] (greatest integer), and similar | 1 | 6/10 | P2 |
| Derivative of inverse trig composites, e.g. d/dx tan⁻¹((1−x)/(1+x)) | 3 | 6/10 | P2 |

**Pattern note.** Rolle's and Mean Value Theorem are deleted, which removed the one "theory" question
from this chapter. It is now purely mechanical — and therefore fully learnable. The
`prove (1−x²)y″ − xy′ = a²y` family (from y = (sin⁻¹x)² or y = e^(a sin⁻¹x)) recurs constantly as a
5- or 3-marker.

### Ch 6. Application of Derivatives

| Topic | Marks | Freq | Priority |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Maxima/minima word problem (volume, area, cost, distance, cone in sphere) | 4–5 | Every year | **P1** |
| Find intervals where f is strictly increasing / decreasing | 3 | Every year | **P1** |
| Show f is increasing/decreasing on a given interval | 2–3 | 8/10 | **P1** |
| Absolute maximum and minimum on a closed interval | 3 | 6/10 | P2 |
| Local maxima/minima by first or second derivative test | 2–3 | 8/10 | **P1** |
| Simple rate of change (radius, area, volume w.r.t. time) | 2 | 6/10 | P2 |
| Case-study framed optimisation | 4 | 7/10 | **P1** |

**Pattern note.** With tangents/normals and approximations deleted, this chapter is now *only*
monotonicity and optimisation. That concentration makes it very high-return: two question types
covering the whole chapter.

The recurring optimisation problems, almost verbatim across years: largest cone inscribed in a
sphere; cylinder of maximum volume in a sphere/cone; open box from a square sheet with corners cut;
window as rectangle + semicircle with fixed perimeter; wire of given length cut into a square and a
circle; shortest distance from a point to a curve; two posts and a wire. Learn these seven and you
have seen the question.

**The trap.** Not verifying it is a maximum. Write the second-derivative test (or a sign table)
explicitly — that is a full mark. Also: answering with the *variable* value when the question asked
for the maximum *volume*.

### Ch 7. Integrals — the single biggest chapter in the paper

| Topic | Marks | Freq | Priority |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Partial fractions | 3–5 | Every year | **P1** |
| Integration by parts (ILATE), incl. ∫eˣ(f + f′)dx | 3 | Every year | **P1** |
| Substitution | 2–3 | Every year | **P1** |
| Definite integral via ∫[0,a] f(x)dx = ∫[0,a] f(a−x)dx | 3 | 9/10 | **P1** |
| 1/(ax²+bx+c) or 1/√(ax²+bx+c) — complete the square | 3 | 9/10 | **P1** |
| ∫ with modulus, e.g. ∫[−1,2]\|x\|dx or \|x−1\| | 2–3 | 7/10 | P2 |
| Odd/even property on symmetric limits | 1–2 | 7/10 | P2 |
| Trig integrals: sin/cos powers, 1/(a + b sin x) type | 3 | 7/10 | P2 |
| (px+q)/√(quadratic) type | 3 | 6/10 | P2 |
| ∫[0,π/2] with the sin↔cos symmetry | 3 | 6/10 | P2 |
| Standard forms straight from the table | 1 | Every year | **P1** |

**Pattern note.** Integrals typically supplies **8–12 marks** of the paper on its own, spread across
one 5-marker, one or two 3-markers, and 1–2 MCQs. It is the highest-return chapter in Mathematics.
Definite-integral-as-a-limit-of-a-sum is deleted, which removed the one genuinely unpleasant topic.

**The trap.** Forgetting `+ C`. Forgetting to change limits after substituting in a *definite*
integral (either change them, or back-substitute — pick one and be consistent). Both are routinely
worth a mark each.

### Ch 8. Application of Integrals

| Topic | Marks | Freq | Priority |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Area bounded by a line and a circle | 5 | 7/10 | **P1** |
| Area bounded by a line and a parabola | 5 | 7/10 | **P1** |
| Area under a simple curve between two ordinates | 3 | 6/10 | P2 |
| Area of a region of an ellipse | 5 | 4/10 | P2 |
| Area using symmetry (multiply a quadrant by 4) | 3–5 | 6/10 | P2 |
| Area bounded by \|x\| or \|y\| type | 3 | 4/10 | P3 |

**Pattern note.** "Area between two curves" in general is deleted; what remains is area under a
simple curve, and area between a **line** and a circle/parabola/ellipse. That is a much smaller and
more predictable target than the old syllabus, but the question is still usually a full 5-marker —
so per-mark it is worth real time.

**The trap.** Not sketching the region. The sketch carries a mark, and without it students routinely
integrate over the wrong interval or forget to split the integral at the intersection point.

### Ch 9. Differential Equations

| Topic | Marks | Freq | Priority |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Linear DE: dy/dx + Py = Q, integrating factor | 3–5 | Every year | **P1** |
| Homogeneous DE of first order and degree (substitute y = vx) | 3–5 | 8/10 | **P1** |
| Variable separable, with a particular solution from an initial condition | 3 | 9/10 | **P1** |
| Order and degree of a given DE | 1 | Every year | **P1** |
| Verify a given function is a solution | 1–2 | 5/10 | P2 |
| Growth/decay or word-problem framing (case study) | 4 | 4/10 | P2 |
| General solution of a simple dy/dx = f(x) | 1–2 | 6/10 | P2 |

**Pattern note.** Formation of a DE from a general solution, and equations reducible to homogeneous
form, are both deleted. So the chapter is now exactly three solving methods. Identify which of the
three you are looking at in the first 10 seconds and this chapter becomes free marks.

**The trap.** Writing the integrating factor as e^∫P dx but then integrating Q instead of Q·(I.F.).
The solution is y·(I.F.) = ∫Q·(I.F.)dx + C. Write that line down as a template before substituting.

---

## Unit IV — Vectors and Three-Dimensional Geometry (14 marks)

### Ch 10. Vector Algebra

| Topic | Marks | Freq | Priority |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Unit vector in the direction of a given vector / along a+b | 1–2 | Every year | **P1** |
| Angle between two vectors using the dot product | 2 | Every year | **P1** |
| Projection of a on b | 1–2 | Every year | **P1** |
| Area of a triangle / parallelogram using the cross product | 2–3 | 9/10 | **P1** |
| Find λ so that two vectors are perpendicular or parallel | 1–2 | 9/10 | **P1** |
| Direction cosines / direction ratios of a vector | 1–2 | 8/10 | **P1** |
| Show \|a+b\| = \|a−b\| ⟺ a ⊥ b, and similar identities | 2–3 | 6/10 | P2 |
| Section formula / position vector of a dividing point | 2 | 6/10 | P2 |
| a·b and a×b of î ĵ k̂ combinations (MCQ) | 1 | Every year | **P1** |
| \|a×b\|² + (a·b)² = \|a\|²\|b\|² | 2 | 4/10 | P3 |

**Pattern note.** Scalar triple product is deleted. What remains is a small, dense formula set that
generates 1- and 2-mark questions in volume — probably the best marks-per-minute in the paper if the
formula box is genuinely memorised.

### Ch 11. Three Dimensional Geometry — **lines only**

| Topic | Marks | Freq | Priority |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Shortest distance between two skew lines | 3–5 | 9/10 | **P1** |
| Angle between two lines (vector or Cartesian form) | 2–3 | 9/10 | **P1** |
| Vector and Cartesian equation of a line through two points | 2–3 | Every year | **P1** |
| Equation of a line through a point, parallel to a given line | 1–2 | 8/10 | **P1** |
| Foot of the perpendicular from a point to a line | 3–5 | 7/10 | **P1** |
| Image (reflection) of a point in a line | 5 | 6/10 | P2 |
| Show two lines intersect; find the point of intersection | 3–5 | 6/10 | P2 |
| Direction cosines of a line; check perpendicularity/parallelism | 1–2 | Every year | **P1** |
| Distance between two parallel lines | 3 | 4/10 | P3 |

**Pattern note.** This is the chapter most distorted by old material. **Every plane topic is deleted**
— no equation of a plane, no angle between planes, no distance of a point from a plane, no
coplanarity. Roughly half of every pre-2023 3D question is therefore out of syllabus. If your
practice source asks for a plane, it is stale.

What replaced that weight is more questions on lines: skew-line distance, foot of perpendicular, and
image of a point are now the standard 5-mark candidates.

---

## Unit V — Linear Programming (5 marks)

### Ch 12. Linear Programming

| Topic | Marks | Freq | Priority |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Graphical solution: maximise/minimise Z, corner-point method | 4–5 | Every year | **P1** |
| Identify the feasible region / corner points from a given graph | 1–2 | 8/10 | **P1** |
| Unbounded feasible region — does max/min exist? | 2–5 | 6/10 | P2 |
| Formulate an LPP from a word problem | 2–3 | 5/10 | P2 |
| Max/min of Z given the corner points (MCQ) | 1 | 8/10 | **P1** |
| Feasible region has no common point → no solution | 1–2 | 4/10 | P3 |

**Pattern note.** Five marks for one completely templated question. Named problem *types* (diet,
transportation, manufacturing) are deleted as categories, and problems are limited to two variables
with at most three non-trivial constraints — which caps how hard this can get. There is no excuse
for losing marks here.

**The trap.** Reading corner points off the graph instead of solving the pair of equations. And, for
an unbounded region, not doing the existence check. Both are single marks that most students drop.

---

## Unit VI — Probability (8 marks)

### Ch 13. Probability

| Topic | Marks | Freq | Priority |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Bayes' theorem word problem | 4–5 | Every year | **P1** |
| Conditional probability P(A\|B) from given data or a table | 2–3 | Every year | **P1** |
| Theorem of total probability | 3–4 | 9/10 | **P1** |
| Independent events — test independence, or compute with it | 2–3 | 9/10 | **P1** |
| Multiplication theorem; drawing without replacement | 2–3 | 8/10 | **P1** |
| Probability distribution of a random variable, and its mean | 3–4 | 7/10 | **P1** |
| At-least / at-most phrasing on two or three trials | 2 | 6/10 | P2 |
| Odds in favour / against, complement | 1 | 5/10 | P2 |

**Pattern note.** **Variance and the Binomial distribution are deleted.** This is the deletion
students most often miss, because the Binomial distribution used to be a guaranteed question. What
survives — and now absorbs the whole 8 marks — is the conditional-probability family: conditional,
multiplication, independence, total probability, Bayes, plus the mean of a random variable.

Bayes is the closest thing to a guaranteed 4- or 5-marker in the paper, and it recurs in a small
number of costumes: two or three machines/factories with different defect rates; two or three bags
with different ball compositions; a diagnostic test with false positives; students from different
sections; a coin chosen from a set of biased coins.

**The trap.** Mixing up P(A|B) and P(B|A). The layout fix in
[`../docs/how-to-answer.md`](../docs/how-to-answer.md) — define events, list all priors, list all
likelihoods, then write the formula — makes this error structurally hard to commit.

---

## Putting it together: a 30-day Maths triage list

Every **P1** row above, and nothing else. That is:

- Matrix method for 3 equations, and A⁻¹ via adjoint
- Integrals: partial fractions, by parts, substitution, complete-the-square, the f(a−x) property
- Linear and variable-separable and homogeneous differential equations
- Maxima–minima word problems, and increasing/decreasing intervals
- Continuity at a point; logarithmic, implicit, parametric and second-order differentiation
- Vectors: unit vector, angle, projection, cross-product area, perpendicularity
- 3D lines: equation through two points, angle between lines, shortest distance, foot of perpendicular
- LP: graphical corner-point method
- Probability: conditional, total probability, Bayes, mean of a random variable
- Relations: equivalence relations; functions: one-one and onto
- Inverse trig: principal values, and sin⁻¹(sin θ) outside the branch
- Area between a line and a circle/parabola

That list is about 60 of 80 marks, and it is genuinely coverable in 30 days.

pyqp.body:
Read [`README.md`](README.md) in this folder for how the Freq and Priority bands are defined and what
they are and are not.

Only **current-syllabus** topics appear here. Deleted topics (potentiometer, cyclotron, LC
oscillations, radioactivity and half-life, resolving power, Zener diode, transistors, logic gates,
optoelectronic devices, hysteresis) are listed in
[`../docs/00-exam-blueprint.md`](../docs/00-exam-blueprint.md) §3.

---

## The 45-mark core

Fifteen question types. Historically these have covered around 45 of 70 marks.

| # | Question type | Chapter | Marks | Freq |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | Series LCR circuit: phasor diagram, impedance, resonance | 7 | 5 | Every year |
| 2 | Young's double slit: fringe-width derivation | 10 | 3–5 | Every year |
| 3 | Refraction through a prism: μ = sin((A+δm)/2)/sin(A/2) | 9 | 3–5 | 9/10 |
| 4 | Gauss's law applied to a wire / sheet / shell | 1 | 3–5 | Every year |
| 5 | Drift velocity → Ohm's law, and resistivity | 3 | 3–5 | Every year |
| 6 | Parallel-plate capacitor with a dielectric; energy stored | 2 | 3–5 | Every year |
| 7 | Compound microscope or astronomical telescope: ray diagram + magnification | 9 | 5 | 9/10 |
| 8 | Photoelectric effect: Einstein's equation + graphs | 11 | 3–4 | Every year |
| 9 | Bohr model: radius and energy of the nᵗʰ orbit; spectral series | 12 | 3–5 | 9/10 |
| 10 | Diode as a half-wave / full-wave rectifier: circuit + waveform | 14 | 3–5 | 9/10 |
| 11 | Biot–Savart applied to a circular loop's axis | 4 | 3–5 | 8/10 |
| 12 | Ampere's circuital law → long straight wire (and the solenoid field) | 4 | 3 | 8/10 |
| 13 | Binding energy per nucleon curve, and what it implies | 13 | 3 | 9/10 |
| 14 | Transformer: principle, working, losses | 7 | 3–5 | 8/10 |
| 15 | Moving-coil galvanometer → ammeter / voltmeter conversion | 4 | 3–5 | 8/10 |

---

## Units I + II — Electrostatics and Current Electricity (16 marks)

### Ch 1. Electric Charges and Fields

| Topic | Marks | Freq | Priority |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Gauss's law: statement, then apply to infinite wire / infinite sheet / spherical shell | 3–5 | Every year | **P1** |
| Electric field on the axial and equatorial line of a dipole | 3–5 | 8/10 | **P1** |
| Torque on a dipole in a uniform field; τ = p × E | 2–3 | 8/10 | **P1** |
| Electric flux through a surface / through a cube face | 1–2 | 9/10 | **P1** |
| Coulomb's law, and force on a charge from two or three others | 2–3 | 7/10 | P2 |
| Electric field lines: properties, and sketching for given charges | 2 | 7/10 | P2 |
| Superposition — net field at a point | 2–3 | 7/10 | P2 |
| Field inside a conductor is zero; charge resides on the surface | 1–2 | 6/10 | P2 |
| Continuous charge distribution, linear/surface/volume charge density | 1 | 5/10 | P2 |

**Pattern note.** Gauss's law is the anchor of this chapter and reappears in three costumes: a long
straight wire (E = λ/2πε₀r), an infinite plane sheet (E = σ/2ε₀), and a uniformly charged thin
spherical shell (E = q/4πε₀r² outside, **zero inside**). The shell's "zero inside" result is asked
as an MCQ or Assertion–Reason almost every year on its own.

**The trap.** Writing the Gaussian surface without justifying *why* that surface (symmetry, and E
parallel/perpendicular to the area vector). That justification is a mark.

### Ch 2. Electrostatic Potential and Capacitance

| Topic | Marks | Freq | Priority |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

| Potential energy of a dipole in a uniform field | 2 | 6/10 | P2 |
| Relation E = −dV/dr | 1–2 | 7/10 | P2 |
| Effect on C, V, Q, E and U when a dielectric is inserted (battery connected vs disconnected) | 3 | 7/10 | **P1** |
| Dielectric polarisation, dielectric constant | 1–2 | 5/10 | P2 |

**Pattern note.** The "insert a dielectric" question is worth singling out. There are two cases and
CBSE asks them interchangeably: **battery still connected** (V constant, so C↑, Q↑, U↑) versus
**battery disconnected** (Q constant, so C↑, V↓, U↓). Students memorise one case and answer the
other. Build a small table for both and learn it as a table.

Van de Graaff generator is deleted.

### Ch 3. Current Electricity

| Topic | Marks | Freq | Priority |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Drift velocity; derive I = neAv_d and hence Ohm's law | 3–5 | Every year | **P1** |
| Resistivity, and its dependence on temperature (conductor vs semiconductor) | 2–3 | 9/10 | **P1** |
| Cells in series and parallel; equivalent emf and internal resistance | 3 | 8/10 | **P1** |

| Wheatstone bridge: balance condition, derived by Kirchhoff | 3–5 | 8/10 | **P1** |
| Metre bridge: circuit, working, finding unknown R | 3 | 6/10 | P2 |

| Mobility; relation between current density, conductivity and E | 1–2 | 7/10 | P2 |

**Pattern note.** The **potentiometer is fully deleted**, theory and practical. That removed a
guaranteed 3–5 mark question and its weight went to Kirchhoff/Wheatstone and to drift velocity. If a
practice paper asks you to compare two cells' emf with a potentiometer, it is an old paper.

**The trap.** In the drift-velocity derivation, students write I = neAv_d and stop. The question asks
you to *hence* obtain Ohm's law — you must substitute v_d = (eE/m)τ and E = V/l to reach
R = ml/(ne²Aτ). The last step is where the marks are.

**Pattern note.** A small chapter that reliably supplies 2–4 marks, mostly in Sections A and B. It is
the best marks-per-page ratio in the book. Make a one-page EM-spectrum table (radio → microwave →
IR → visible → UV → X-ray → gamma, with wavelength range, source, detector, use) and learn it cold —

**Pattern note.** Ray Optics alone typically carries **8–10 marks**, and it is the one chapter that
appears in every section of the paper — MCQ, 2-mark, 3-mark derivation, case study, and 5-mark
instrument question. It is the highest-priority chapter in Physics, full stop.

**The trap — sign convention.** More marks are lost to sign convention in this chapter than to
anything else in the paper. Fix the rule once: distances measured from the pole/optical centre, in
the direction of incident light positive, against it negative; heights above the axis positive. Write
`u = −30 cm` explicitly rather than substituting 30 and hoping.

**The trap — ray diagrams.** They must show at least two rays, arrowheads on every ray, the image
clearly located, and all of F, 2F, O and C labelled. The diagram is worth 1–2 of the 5 marks on the
instrument questions and is marked independently of the algebra.

**Pattern note.** Resolving power of a microscope and telescope, validity of ray optics, and
polarisation by scattering are deleted. The chapter is now essentially **Huygens + YDSE +
single-slit diffraction**, and YDSE fringe width is one of the two or three most reliably asked
results in the whole paper.

Two syllabus qualifiers matter here. The fringe width is listed as "**no derivation, final expression
only**", and the width of the central maximum as "**qualitative treatment only**" — so the formulas
and their consequences (what happens when λ, D, d or the slit width changes) are worth far more of
your time than the derivations. The **polarisation block has been trimmed** across recent revisions
and sources disagree on what survives; treat it as low priority and check the current syllabus PDF.
See [`../physics/10-wave-optics.md`](../physics/10-wave-optics.md) §1.

**Pattern note.** Highly formulaic and therefore high-return — one equation
(hν = φ₀ + ½mv²_max = φ₀ + eV₀) plus two graphs generates nearly every question. Case-study
questions in Section D draw on this chapter often, using the graphs as the "source".

**What the graph question actually wants:** for stopping potential V₀ vs frequency ν, the slope is
**h/e** and the x-intercept is the **threshold frequency**; the line's slope is the *same* for all
metals and only the intercept changes. That is the asked fact.

### Ch 14. Semiconductor Electronics

| Topic | Marks | Freq | Priority |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |

| p-n junction formation: depletion region and barrier potential | 2–3 | 9/10 | **P1** |
| Diode I–V characteristics in forward and reverse bias; how to obtain them | 2–3 | 9/10 | **P1** |

**Pattern note.** **Read this even if you read nothing else on this page.** Zener diode, LED,
photodiode, solar cell, transistors and logic gates are all deleted. What is left is five topics —
and it still carries **7 marks**, a full 10% of the paper.

That makes Ch 14 the highest marks-per-hour chapter in Physics by a wide margin. Students skip it
because it is the last chapter in the book and because they remember it as "the hard transistor
chapter" from seniors. It no longer is. Two focused days here is worth more than two weeks on
Magnetism and Matter.

**The rectifier question specifics.** You need: the circuit diagram (with the transformer and load
resistance shown), the input waveform, and the output waveform, correctly aligned. For the full-wave
rectifier, show that output pulses appear for **both** half-cycles. The three diagrams are the bulk
of the marks; the explanation is one or two lines.

## Putting it together: a 30-day Physics triage list

Every **P1** row above. In chapter order:

- **Ch 1:** Gauss's law + three applications; dipole field; flux
- **Ch 2:** parallel-plate capacitor ± dielectric; energy stored; series/parallel; potential; equipotentials
- **Ch 3:** drift velocity → Ohm's law; resistivity vs temperature; Kirchhoff; Wheatstone; cells; internal resistance
- **Ch 4:** Biot–Savart for a loop; Ampere's law → long straight wire; galvanometer conversion; F = I(l×B); F = q(v×B)
- **Ch 5:** Earth's magnetic elements only
- **Ch 6:** Faraday and Lenz; motional emf; self-inductance; AC generator; direction of induced current
- **Ch 7:** series LCR + phasor; resonance and Q; transformer; power factor; pure L and pure C
- **Ch 8:** displacement current; EM spectrum table; properties of EM waves
- **Ch 9 (do this first):** prism formula; lens maker's formula; mirror formula; TIR; power and combination; microscope; telescope; sign-convention numericals
- **Ch 10:** YDSE fringe width; single-slit diffraction; conditions for interference; effect of changing λ/D/d
- **Ch 11:** Einstein's equation; the two graphs; work function numericals; de Broglie
- **Ch 12:** Bohr's postulates; E_n = −13.6/n²; spectral series; energy level diagram
- **Ch 13:** BE/nucleon curve; mass defect numericals; fission and fusion; R = R₀A^(1/3)
- **Ch 14:** the whole chapter

That is roughly 45–50 of 70 marks, and Ch 9 + Ch 14 + Ch 7 alone are about 25 of them.

Everything in the current syllabus, on one page. **Deleted topics are not here** — if a formula you
half-remember is missing, check [`../docs/00-exam-blueprint.md`](../docs/00-exam-blueprint.md) §3
before hunting for it; it is probably out of syllabus.

Use this for the daily 20-minute revision in February, and read it once on the morning of the exam.

## Ch 1 — Relations and Functions

```
Reflexive    : (a, a) ∈ R for every a ∈ A
Symmetric    : (a, b) ∈ R ⟹ (b, a) ∈ R
Transitive   : (a, b), (b, c) ∈ R ⟹ (a, c) ∈ R
Equivalence  : all three

One-one (injective) : f(x₁) = f(x₂) ⟹ x₁ = x₂       [or f′ of one sign throughout]
Onto (surjective)   : range = codomain
Bijective           : both

Equivalence class  [a] = { x ∈ A : (a, x) ∈ R };  classes partition A

|A| = m, |B| = n :
  relations A→B     = 2^(mn)          relations on A (|A| = n) = 2^(n²)
  reflexive on A    = 2^(n² − n)      symmetric on A           = 2^(n(n+1)/2)
  functions A→B     = n^m             one-one A→B (m ≤ n)      = n!/(n − m)!
  bijections A→A    = n!
```

## Ch 2 — Inverse Trigonometric Functions

```
              DOMAIN            RANGE (principal value branch)
sin⁻¹ x      [−1, 1]           [−π/2, π/2]
cos⁻¹ x      [−1, 1]           [0, π]
tan⁻¹ x      R                 (−π/2, π/2)
cot⁻¹ x      R                 (0, π)
sec⁻¹ x      |x| ≥ 1           [0, π] − {π/2}
cosec⁻¹ x    |x| ≥ 1           [−π/2, π/2] − {0}

Family A (sin⁻¹, tan⁻¹, cosec⁻¹) : f(−x) = −f(x)
Family B (cos⁻¹, cot⁻¹, sec⁻¹)   : f(−x) = π − f(x)      ← never negative

sin⁻¹(sin θ) = θ  ONLY if θ ∈ [−π/2, π/2] ;  else reduce
cos⁻¹(cos θ) = θ  ONLY if θ ∈ [0, π]      ;  else reduce
tan⁻¹(tan θ) = θ  ONLY if θ ∈ (−π/2, π/2) ;  else reduce

sin⁻¹x + cos⁻¹x = π/2

sin(cos⁻¹x) = √(1 − x²)      tan(sin⁻¹x) = x/√(1 − x²)      sec(tan⁻¹x) = √(1 + x²)
```

## Ch 3 — Matrices

```
Order m × n → mn elements ;  a_ij = row i, column j
Number of possible orders for k elements = number of divisors of k
Number of m × n matrices with entries from a set of size s = s^(mn)

AB defined iff cols(A) = rows(B) ;  A(m×n) B(n×p) = AB(m×p)

(A′)′ = A      (kA)′ = kA′      (A + B)′ = A′ + B′      (AB)′ = B′A′

Symmetric      : A′ = A
Skew-symmetric : A′ = −A  ⟹  all diagonal entries = 0  ⟹  trace = 0
A = ½(A + A′) + ½(A − A′)                [symmetric + skew-symmetric]

A + A′, AA′, A′A are symmetric ;  A − A′ is skew-symmetric
A, B symmetric ⟹ AB + BA symmetric, AB − BA skew-symmetric

AB ≠ BA in general ;  AB = O does NOT imply A = O or B = O
(A + B)² = A² + AB + BA + B²             [NOT A² + 2AB + B²]

For 2 × 2 :  A² − (trace A)·A + (det A)·I = O
```

## Ch 4 — Determinants

```
2 × 2 :  |A| = ad − bc

3 × 3 :  expand along the row/column with the most zeros
         signs :   + − +
                   − + −
                   + − +

Minor M_ij    : delete row i, column j
Cofactor A_ij = (−1)^(i+j) M_ij

adj A = TRANSPOSE of the cofactor matrix
A (adj A) = (adj A) A = |A| I
A⁻¹ = (1/|A|) adj A                      (requires |A| ≠ 0)

2 × 2 shortcut : adj [[a, b], [c, d]] = [[d, −b], [−c, a]]

|AB| = |A||B|        |Aᵀ| = |A|          |kA| = kⁿ|A|        |Aⁿ| = |A|ⁿ
|A⁻¹| = 1/|A|        |adj A| = |A|^(n−1)
adj(AB) = (adj B)(adj A)                 (AB)⁻¹ = B⁻¹A⁻¹
det of a skew-symmetric matrix of ODD order = 0

Area of triangle = ½ | det [[x₁,y₁,1],[x₂,y₂,1],[x₃,y₃,1]] |
Collinear ⟺ that determinant = 0

AX = B → X = A⁻¹B if |A| ≠ 0                      (unique solution, consistent)
|A| = 0 and (adj A)B ≠ O  → inconsistent, no solution
|A| = 0 and (adj A)B = O  → infinitely many, or none
```

## Ch 5 — Continuity and Differentiability

```
CONTINUOUS at a  : LHL = RHL = f(a)
   LHL = lim f(a − h),  RHL = lim f(a + h),  h → 0⁺

DIFFERENTIABLE at a : LHD = RHD, both finite
   differentiable ⟹ continuous ;  continuous ⇏ differentiable  (|x| at 0)

DERIVATIVES
  xⁿ → n x^(n−1)          log x → 1/x            log_a x → 1/(x log a)
  eˣ → eˣ                 aˣ → aˣ log a          constant → 0

  sin x → cos x            cos x → −sin x
  tan x → sec²x            cot x → −cosec²x
  sec x → sec x tan x      cosec x → −cosec x cot x

  sin⁻¹x → 1/√(1 − x²)     cos⁻¹x → −1/√(1 − x²)
  tan⁻¹x → 1/(1 + x²)      cot⁻¹x → −1/(1 + x²)
  sec⁻¹x → 1/(|x|√(x²−1))  cosec⁻¹x → −1/(|x|√(x²−1))

RULES
  Chain    : dy/dx = f′(g(x)) · g′(x)
  Product  : (uv)′ = u′v + uv′
  Quotient : (u/v)′ = (u′v − uv′)/v²
  Implicit : differentiate both sides; every y term gains a dy/dx
  Log diff : variable in base AND exponent → take log first
  Parametric : dy/dx = (dy/dt)/(dx/dt)
               d²y/dx² = [ d/dt (dy/dx) ] / (dx/dt)     ← divide AGAIN

STANDARD LIMITS
  lim (sin x)/x = 1     lim (tan x)/x = 1     lim (eˣ − 1)/x = 1     lim (1+x)^(1/x) = e
  x→0                   x→0                    x→0                    x→0

"PROVE A RELATION" METHOD
  differentiate → clear the radical → SQUARE both sides → differentiate → divide by 2y′
```

## Ch 6 — Application of Derivatives

```
RATES : dy/dt = (dy/dx)(dx/dt).  Always state units.

  Circle   A = πr² → dA/dt = 2πr dr/dt      C = 2πr → dC/dt = 2π dr/dt
  Sphere   V = (4/3)πr³ → dV/dt = 4πr² dr/dt    S = 4πr² → dS/dt = 8πr dr/dt
  Cube     V = x³ → dV/dt = 3x² dx/dt       S = 6x² → dS/dt = 12x dx/dt

MONOTONICITY
  f′(x) > 0 on I ⟹ strictly increasing        f′(x) < 0 on I ⟹ strictly decreasing
  Method: f′ → factorise → critical points → sign table → state intervals

EXTREMA
  Critical point : f′(c) = 0 or f′(c) undefined
  1st derivative test : f′ goes + → − ⟹ MAX ;  − → + ⟹ MIN ;  no change ⟹ inflection
  2nd derivative test : f′(c) = 0 and f″(c) < 0 ⟹ MAX ;  f″(c) > 0 ⟹ MIN ;  = 0 ⟹ test fails
  Absolute extrema on [a, b] : compare f at critical points AND at both endpoints

STANDARD OPTIMISATION RESULTS
  Open box from square sheet of side a, corners x cut  →  x = a/6
  Max-area rectangle in a circle                       →  a SQUARE
  Max-volume cylinder in a sphere of radius R          →  h = 2R/√3
  Max-volume cone in a sphere of radius R              →  h = 4R/3
  Window (rectangle + semicircle), perimeter P         →  height = radius = P/(4 + π)
  Wire length L cut into square + circle, min area     →  circle piece = Lπ/(π + 4)
  Fixed sum, min sum of squares/cubes                  →  the numbers are EQUAL
```

## Ch 7 — Integrals

```
STANDARD
  ∫ xⁿ dx = x^(n+1)/(n+1) + C   (n ≠ −1)      ∫ dx/x = log|x| + C
  ∫ eˣ dx = eˣ + C                            ∫ aˣ dx = aˣ/log a + C

  ∫ sin x dx = −cos x + C                     ∫ cos x dx = sin x + C
  ∫ sec²x dx = tan x + C                      ∫ cosec²x dx = −cot x + C
  ∫ sec x tan x dx = sec x + C                ∫ cosec x cot x dx = −cosec x + C
  ∫ tan x dx = log|sec x| + C                 ∫ cot x dx = log|sin x| + C
  ∫ sec x dx = log|sec x + tan x| + C         ∫ cosec x dx = log|cosec x − cot x| + C
  ∫ dx/√(1 − x²) = sin⁻¹x + C                 ∫ dx/(1 + x²) = tan⁻¹x + C

THE NINE SPECIAL FORMS
  ∫ dx/(x² − a²)  = (1/2a) log|(x − a)/(x + a)| + C
  ∫ dx/(a² − x²)  = (1/2a) log|(a + x)/(a − x)| + C
  ∫ dx/(x² + a²)  = (1/a) tan⁻¹(x/a) + C

  ∫ dx/√(x² − a²) = log|x + √(x² − a²)| + C
  ∫ dx/√(x² + a²) = log|x + √(x² + a²)| + C
  ∫ dx/√(a² − x²) = sin⁻¹(x/a) + C

  ∫ √(a² − x²) dx = (x/2)√(a² − x²) + (a²/2) sin⁻¹(x/a) + C
  ∫ √(x² + a²) dx = (x/2)√(x² + a²) + (a²/2) log|x + √(x² + a²)| + C
  ∫ √(x² − a²) dx = (x/2)√(x² − a²) − (a²/2) log|x + √(x² − a²)| + C     ← MINUS

BY PARTS
  ∫ u v dx = u ∫v dx − ∫ (du/dx)(∫v dx) dx
  ILATE : Inverse, Log, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential   (choose u = the earlier one)
  ∫ log x dx = x log x − x + C
  ∫ eˣ [ f(x) + f′(x) ] dx = eˣ f(x) + C

PARTIAL FRACTIONS (numerator degree < denominator degree; else divide first)
  (x−a)(x−b)              → A/(x−a) + B/(x−b)
  (x−a)²                  → A/(x−a) + B/(x−a)²
  (x−a)(x−b)(x−c)         → A/(x−a) + B/(x−b) + C/(x−c)
  (x−a)²(x−b)             → A/(x−a) + B/(x−a)² + C/(x−b)
  (x−a)(x²+bx+c) irred.   → A/(x−a) + (Bx + C)/(x²+bx+c)

TRIG REDUCTION
  sin²x = (1 − cos 2x)/2        cos²x = (1 + cos 2x)/2
  sin 2x = 2 sin x cos x        cos 2x = 1 − 2sin²x = 2cos²x − 1
  2 sin A cos B = sin(A+B) + sin(A−B)
  2 cos A cos B = cos(A+B) + cos(A−B)
  2 sin A sin B = cos(A−B) − cos(A+B)

DEFINITE INTEGRAL PROPERTIES
  ∫[a,b] f = −∫[b,a] f  ;  ∫[a,a] f = 0
  ∫[a,b] f = ∫[a,c] f + ∫[c,b] f
  ∫[a,b] f(x)dx = ∫[a,b] f(a + b − x)dx
  ∫[0,a] f(x)dx = ∫[0,a] f(a − x)dx                        ← the workhorse
  ∫[0,2a] f = ∫[0,a] f(x)dx + ∫[0,a] f(2a − x)dx
  ∫[0,2a] f = 2∫[0,a] f  if f(2a − x) = f(x) ;  = 0 if f(2a − x) = −f(x)
  ∫[−a,a] f = 2∫[0,a] f  if f EVEN ;  = 0 if f ODD

  NO +C in a definite integral.  Change the limits when you substitute.
```

## Ch 8 — Application of Integrals

```
Area (strips ∥ y-axis) = ∫[a,b] y dx
Area (strips ∥ x-axis) = ∫[c,d] x dy

Below the axis → split at the crossing point and take |absolute value| of each piece

Circle  x² + y² = a²          area = πa²  ;  quadrant = πa²/4
Ellipse x²/a² + y²/b² = 1     area = πab  ;  quadrant = πab/4
Parabola y² = 4ax             symmetric about the x-axis (double the upper half)
Parabola x² = 4ay             symmetric about the y-axis

∫[0,a] √(a² − x²) dx = πa²/4

Sector of a circle, angle θ (radians) = (θ/2π) πa² = ½a²θ

PROCEDURE: sketch → intersections → shade → choose variable → limits → evaluate → "square units"
```

## Ch 9 — Differential Equations

```
ORDER  = order of the highest derivative
DEGREE = power of the highest-order derivative, after clearing radicals and fractions
         NOT DEFINED if the equation is not polynomial in its derivatives
         (contains sin(dy/dx), log(dy/dx), e^(dy/dx))

VARIABLES SEPARABLE : f(y)dy = g(x)dx  → integrate both sides, one +C

HOMOGENEOUS : dy/dx = F(y/x)
  put y = vx  and  dy/dx = v + x dv/dx     ← the "+v" is essential
  separate in v and x, integrate, then substitute v = y/x back
  (if naturally dx/dy = F(x/y), put x = vy instead)

LINEAR : dy/dx + P(x)y = Q(x)
  I.F. = e^(∫P dx)
  y · (I.F.) = ∫ Q · (I.F.) dx + C          ← Q TIMES the I.F.

  y-version : dx/dy + P(y)x = Q(y),  I.F. = e^(∫P dy),  x·(I.F.) = ∫Q·(I.F.)dy + C

I.F. SHORTCUTS
  P = k      → e^(kx)        P = 1/x   → x         P = n/x   → xⁿ
  P = −1/x   → 1/x           P = tan x → sec x     P = cot x → sin x
  P = −tan x → cos x

GROWTH/DECAY : dN/dt = kN  →  N = N₀ e^(kt)
```

## Ch 10 — Vector Algebra

```
|a| = √(a₁² + a₂² + a₃²)          â = a/|a|
AB = b − a                        (head minus tail)

Section formula (A(a), B(b), ratio m : n)
  internal : r = (mb + na)/(m + n)      external : r = (mb − na)/(m − n)
  midpoint : r = (a + b)/2

Direction cosines : l = a₁/|a|, m = a₂/|a|, n = a₃/|a| ;   l² + m² + n² = 1

DOT (scalar)
  a·b = |a||b| cos θ = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + a₃b₃           a·a = |a|²
  cos θ = a·b / (|a||b|)
  perpendicular ⟺ a·b = 0
  projection of a on b = a·b/|b|                    (a SCALAR, may be negative)
  vector projection of a on b = [ (a·b)/|b|² ] b
  î·î = ĵ·ĵ = k̂·k̂ = 1 ;  î·ĵ = ĵ·k̂ = k̂·î = 0

CROSS (vector)
  a × b = determinant with rows  î ĵ k̂ / a₁ a₂ a₃ / b₁ b₂ b₃
        = î(a₂b₃ − a₃b₂) − ĵ(a₁b₃ − a₃b₁) + k̂(a₁b₂ − a₂b₁)    ← middle term MINUS
  |a × b| = |a||b| sin θ           a × b = −(b × a)          a × a = 0
  parallel ⟺ a × b = 0
  î×ĵ = k̂,  ĵ×k̂ = î,  k̂×î = ĵ

  area of parallelogram (adjacent sides a, b) = |a × b|
  area of parallelogram (diagonals d₁, d₂)    = ½ |d₁ × d₂|
  area of triangle (two sides a, b)           = ½ |a × b|
  unit vector ⊥ to both a and b               = (a × b)/|a × b|

|a × b|² + (a·b)² = |a|² |b|²
|a + b| = |a − b|  ⟺  a ⊥ b
a, b, c unit with a + b + c = 0  ⟹  a·b + b·c + c·a = −3/2
```

## Ch 11 — Three Dimensional Geometry (lines only)

```
DRs of AB = (x₂ − x₁, y₂ − y₁, z₂ − z₁) ;  divide by |AB| for direction cosines

LINE through A(a) with direction b :
  vector    : r = a + λb
  Cartesian : (x − x₁)/a₁ = (y − y₁)/a₂ = (z − z₁)/a₃
  general point : (a₁λ + x₁, a₂λ + y₁, a₃λ + z₁)

LINE through A(a) and B(b) : r = a + λ(b − a)
  Cartesian : (x − x₁)/(x₂ − x₁) = (y − y₁)/(y₂ − y₁) = (z − z₁)/(z₂ − z₁)

ANGLE between two lines : cos θ = |b₁·b₂| / (|b₁||b₂|)          ← MODULUS
  perpendicular : a₁a₂ + b₁b₂ + c₁c₂ = 0
  parallel      : a₁/a₂ = b₁/b₂ = c₁/c₂

SKEW LINES : neither parallel nor intersecting

SHORTEST DISTANCE
  skew     : d = | (b₁ × b₂) · (a₂ − a₁) | / | b₁ × b₂ |
  parallel : d = | b × (a₂ − a₁) | / | b |
  d = 0 ⟹ the lines intersect

FOOT OF PERPENDICULAR from P : general point Q(λ) → PQ·b = 0 → solve λ → Q
IMAGE of P in the line        : P′ = 2Q − P

Before reading DRs, normalise so the coefficient of x, y, z inside each bracket is 1:
  (2y − 1)/4 = (y − ½)/2
```

## Ch 12 — Linear Programming

```
Z = ax + by  (objective function) ;  inequalities are the constraints

CORNER-POINT METHOD
  1. all constraints, including x ≥ 0, y ≥ 0
  2. boundary lines and their intercepts
  3. graph on graph paper, scale stated, lines labelled
  4. shade the feasible region (test the origin in each inequality)
  5. corner points by SOLVING SIMULTANEOUS EQUATIONS — not by reading the graph
  6. table of Z at each corner point
  7. state the optimum: value, point, and max/min

BOUNDED region   → both max and min exist, at corner points
UNBOUNDED region → may not exist; CHECK:
  M is the max ⟺ ax + by > M has no point in common with the feasible region
  m is the min ⟺ ax + by < m has no point in common with the feasible region

Equal Z at two corner points → infinitely many optima, all along that segment
Contradictory constraints     → empty feasible region → no feasible solution
```

## Ch 13 — Probability

```
CONDITIONAL : P(A|B) = P(A ∩ B)/P(B),  P(B) ≠ 0        ← "given" is the DENOMINATOR
  P(A′|B) = 1 − P(A|B)
  P((A ∪ C)|B) = P(A|B) + P(C|B) − P((A ∩ C)|B)

MULTIPLICATION : P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B|A) = P(B)P(A|B)
  P(A ∩ B ∩ C) = P(A) P(B|A) P(C|A ∩ B)               ← "without replacement"

INDEPENDENT : P(A ∩ B) = P(A)P(B)  ⟺  P(A|B) = P(A)
  P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A)P(B)
  P(neither) = (1 − P(A))(1 − P(B))
  P(at least one) = 1 − P(neither)
  independent ≠ mutually exclusive
  mutually exclusive with non-zero probabilities ⟹ NOT independent

ADDITION : P(A ∪ B) = P(A) + P(B) − P(A ∩ B)

TOTAL PROBABILITY : P(A) = Σᵢ P(Eᵢ) P(A|Eᵢ)          (E₁…Eₙ a partition)

BAYES : P(Eᵢ|A) = P(Eᵢ)P(A|Eᵢ) / Σⱼ P(Eⱼ)P(A|Eⱼ)
  LAYOUT: define events → all priors → all likelihoods → formula → substitute
  P(Eᵢ) are PRIORS ; P(Eᵢ|A) are POSTERIORS

RANDOM VARIABLE
  Σ pᵢ = 1  and  pᵢ ≥ 0                               ← use this to find an unknown constant
  Mean = E(X) = Σ xᵢ pᵢ
  (Variance and the Binomial distribution are OUT of syllabus)
```

---

## The last-page checklist, for the exam hall

Before you hand the paper in:

1. `+ C` on every indefinite integral; **no** `+ C` on any definite integral.
2. Every vector answer written with î ĵ k̂ or an arrow.
3. Every area answered in "square units"; every rate with its unit.
4. Every graph: axes labelled, scale stated, region shaded, corner points named.
5. Every "prove" ended with an explicit concluding line.
6. Abandoned internal-choice attempts crossed out.
7. Question numbers matching the paper.
8. Modulus signs present in log answers, and in the angle-between-lines formula.
